column1: # The differences between Wireshark and the crate that were triaged, which do not fail the run
# (compare.py). A difference that no row explains fails it.
# Columns, separated by tabs: what (the kind of difference, `*` for any: header, ie, field,
# ws-malformed, crate-refuses, class), where (a regular expression over the text of the
# difference), verdict (wireshark: Wireshark reads the octets otherwise than the clause;
# crate-by-clause: the crate does what the clause says and Wireshark shows something else;
# both: both find fault, or read them as the clause allows; gap: Wireshark 4.6.4 does not
# dissect or name them), and the reference: the clause of TS 29.244 V19.6.0, and why.

column4: §7.6.9, §7.6.10: a receiver discards an IE that its scope does not have, the repetitions of an IE that it has once, and an IE of a type that it does not have, whose value the crate does not read (check() tells each); Wireshark dissects it, and finds it malformed
§7.6.7: an IE whose Length runs past its scope has an invalid length, where the crate stops; Wireshark finds the octets malformed
§7.6.8: a value that does not decode, which the crate keeps as octets and check() tells; Wireshark finds it malformed

Table 8.1.2-1: IE type 0 is Reserved, and a receiver discards an IE of a type that it does not have (§7.6.9): check() tells it, or its scope, or the IE does not frame; Wireshark reports it as an error

column2: ^IE [0-9/]*\b27: \(Error/Protocol\): IE wrongly encoded \(the crate decodes it\)$
column4: Table 8.1.2-1: GBR is Extendable with 10 fixed octets, and a receiver ignores the octets after its fields (§8.1.2); Wireshark 4.6.4 reports a GBR of more octets as wrongly encoded

column2: Wireshark dissects it, the crate stops: IE type \d+ has the Length \d+, and \d+ octets follow its header
column4: §7.6.7: an IE whose Length runs past the grouped IE that holds it has an invalid length, which check() tells; Wireshark 4.6.4 dissects the octets that there are, and reports no error

column2: ^the IEs do not fit the message: IE type \d+ has the Length \d+, and \d+ octets follow its header
column4: §7.6.7: an IE whose Length runs past the message has an invalid length; Wireshark 4.6.4 dissects the octets that there are, and reports no error

column2: ^the Message Length is \d+, and \d+ octets follow the first four
column4: §6.5, §7.6.3: Message::decode reads one message, and refuses octets after its Message Length, as a receiver of one message answers "Invalid length"; Message::decode_datagram reads them as the next message of a bundle, as Wireshark does

column2: ^IE none: .*\(the crate reads a message of a type that no table has\)$
column4: §7.6.4: a message of a type that the receiver does not have is discarded, which check() tells; Wireshark 4.6.4 finds the message malformed

column2: ^IE [0-9/]*\b45: \(Error/Malformed\): Malformed Packet \(Exception occurred\) \(the crate decodes it\)$
column4: §8.2.27: a Downlink Data Service Information of QFII alone has the QFI after its flags, which the crate decodes; Wireshark 4.6.4 finds it malformed
§8.2.4, §8.2.117: a label is the octets after its length, and may hold a zero octet; Wireshark 4.6.4 shows the name up to its first zero octet
§8.2.216: PDUSM is bit 4 of octet 5; Wireshark 4.6.4 reads it with the mask of EML4S, bit 3
§8.2.223: N6JMI is bit 3 of octet 5; Wireshark 4.6.4 reads it with the mask of DLPMI, bit 2
§8.2.101: the IMSI and the IMEI are TBCD (TS 29.274 §8.3), whose codes 1010 to 1110 are *, #, a, b and c (TS 29.002): the crate writes them, Wireshark 4.6.4 shows ?
§8.2.101: an IMSI, IMEI or NAI that is no TBCD of its digits or no text, a filler before its last digit for instance, the crate keeps as octets; Wireshark 4.6.4 shows the digits before it
Table 8.2.1-1: Causes 90 to 92 are of PFD Partial Failure Information, which Wireshark 4.6.4 does not name
